summary: In this workshop, Apoorva Joshi introduces AI agents and guides attendees through building a multimodal AI agent from scratch in Python. The presentation defines an AI agent as a system using a Large Language Model (LLM) to reason, create plans, and execute them with tools. Three paradigms of LLM interaction are contrasted: simple prompting (parametric knowledge only), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (external knowledge but no self-refinement), and agents (autonomy for complex, multi-step tasks via tools and reasoning). Joshi cautions that agents incur higher costs and latency, recommending them only for unstructured, complex workflows. The four core components are detailed: perception (inputs like text and images), planning/reasoning (Chain of Thought and ReAct patterns), tools (external interfaces with schemas that LLMs identify but code executes), and memory (short-term for single conversations, long-term for persistent personalization). A worked weather-query example illustrates the full tool-calling flow. The workshop then pivots to multimodality—models that process, understand, and generate diverse data types including text, images, audio, and video. Two classes of multimodal models are introduced: multimodal embedding models and multimodal LLMs. A multimodal agent combines a multimodal LLM with tools to search multimodal data and reason over it. The agent to be built has two objectives: answer questions about a large document corpus and explain or analyze charts. The key challenge is retrieving information from documents with text interleaved with images and tables. Traditional approaches face limitations including loss of context at chunk boundaries, pipeline complexity, and the modality gap in CLIP-based architectures. A newer VLM-based architecture uses a single encoder for both modalities, preserving contextual relationships. The simplified pipeline takes a screenshot per document page, passes it through a multimodal embedding model, and stores the embedding with the image path as metadata in a vector database. Q&A addresses overlap strategies, the 'lost in the middle' problem, model selection, and handling weakly aligned modalities like time series. The agent's workflow is then detailed: a query is forwarded to a multimodal LLM (Gemini 2.0 Flash) equipped with a vector search tool; the LLM decides whether to call the tool; vector search returns references to screenshots stored in blob storage rather than images themselves; the agent fetches screenshots and passes them with the query and conversation history to the LLM, which generates a final answer. The agent may also decide no tool is needed. Short-term memory is implemented using session IDs to retrieve and update chat history in a database, logging at minimum user queries and LLM responses, with optional logging of tool calls and reasoning traces. The workshop concludes with a hands-on lab accessible via a GitHub repository, offering either a fill-in-code notebook (lab.ipynb) or a pre-filled solutions notebook (solutions.ipynb), with roughly 10 minutes for setup and about 45 minutes for the lab itself.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: AI agents use LLMs to reason, plan, and execute complex, multi-step tasks using tools, offering advantages over simple prompting and RAG but at higher cost and latency.
The four components of an AI agent are perception, planning/reasoning, tools, and memory (short-term and long-term).
VLM-based architectures use a single encoder for both text and visual data, preserving contextual relationships and simplifying the pipeline to screenshot-based embeddings.

The agent workflow forwards a query to a multimodal LLM (Gemini 2.0 Flash) with a vector search tool; vector search returns screenshot references, and the agent fetches images from blob storage to pass to the LLM along with query and history.
Short-term memory uses session IDs to retrieve conversation history from a database before each LLM call and logs responses and queries back, with optional logging of tool calls and reasoning traces.
The LLM may decide not to call a tool if the query does not require retrieval, directly generating an answer.
The lab provides two notebooks: lab.ipynb for writing code with inline reference documentation, and solutions.ipynb with all code pre-filled.
Weakly aligned modalities like time series data require different retrieval strategies and cannot easily share a vector space with text and images.
Understand the differences between simple prompting, RAG, and AI agents.
Identify the appropriate use cases and trade-offs for deploying AI agents.

sections.title: Introduction and Workshop Overview
sections.summary: Apoorva Joshi introduces the workshop on building multimodal AI agents from scratch in Python, outlining the structure and expectations for the session.

sections.title: What are AI Agents and Why Do We Need Them?
sections.summary: Defines AI agents and contrasts three paradigms: simple prompting, RAG, and agents. Discusses the trade-offs of agents, including higher cost and latency.

sections.title: Components of AI Agents: Perception, Planning, and Tools
sections.summary: Details the first three components of agents. Perception handles inputs like text and images. Planning uses LLMs with patterns like Chain of Thought and ReAct. Tools are external interfaces defined by schemas that LLMs call but do not execute directly.

sections.title: Components of AI Agents: Memory
sections.summary: Explains the memory component, categorizing it into short-term for single conversations and long-term for storing, updating, and retrieving information over time.

sections.title: Tool-Calling Agent Example and Multimodality Introduction
sections.summary: Walks through a weather-query example illustrating the full tool-calling agent flow. Introduces multimodality as the ability of ML models to process, understand, and generate different data types, with the lab focusing on text and images. Presents real-world examples of mixed-media data.

sections.title: Multimodal Models and the Multimodal Agent
sections.summary: Introduces two classes of multimodal models: multimodal embedding models for unified search and multimodal LLMs for multi-format input/output. Defines a multimodal agent as a multimodal LLM with tools to search multimodal data and reason over it.

sections.title: Agent Objectives and Multimodal Data Preparation Challenges
sections.summary: Describes the agent's two objectives: answering questions about a large document corpus and explaining charts. Explains the challenge of retrieving information from mixed-modality documents and outlines two traditional processing approaches with their limitations.

sections.title: VLM-Based Architecture and Simplified Pipeline
sections.summary: Introduces VLM-based architectures that use a single encoder for text and images, eliminating the modality gap and preserving contextual relationships. Details the simplified data preparation pipeline: screenshot each page, embed with a multimodal embedding model, store path as metadata, and save to MongoDB. Includes audience Q&A on the screenshot approach.

sections.title: Q&A on Screenshot Approach, Model Selection, and Weakly Aligned Modalities
sections.summary: Extended Q&A addresses overlap strategies for screenshots, metadata pre-filtering, the 'lost in the middle' problem justifying retrieval over full-document ingestion, model selection rationale (any VLM-based model avoids the CLIP modality gap), running models locally, and handling weakly aligned modalities like time series data, which require different retrieval strategies.

sections.title: Agent Workflow and Memory Management
sections.summary: Details the agent's workflow: query forwarded to a multimodal LLM (Gemini 2.0 Flash) with a vector search tool and conversation history; vector search returns screenshot references rather than images; agent fetches screenshots from blob storage; images, query, and history are passed to the LLM to generate an answer. The LLM may decide no tool is needed. Short-term memory uses session IDs to retrieve and update chat history in a database, logging at minimum queries and LLM responses, optionally tool calls and reasoning traces.

sections.title: Hands-On Lab Instructions
sections.summary: Directs attendees to a GitHub repository for the hands-on lab, recommending running it locally. Two notebooks are provided: lab.ipynb for writing code with inline reference documentation, and solutions.ipynb with all code pre-filled. Setup takes about 10 minutes, with approximately 45 minutes for the lab. The presenter and team are available for questions.

demonstrations: Workshop attendees build a multimodal AI agent from scratch using Python.
Demonstration of a weather tool schema including name, description, and string parameter for city.
Worked example of a simple tool-calling agent handling a weather query for San Francisco, showing the full flow from query to final response.
Data preparation pipeline: convert documents to page-level screenshots, embed with a multimodal embedding model, store embeddings and image paths in MongoDB.
Detailed walkthrough of the multimodal agent workflow from query intake through vector search, blob storage retrieval, and final answer generation.
Hands-on lab with two notebook options: lab.ipynb for writing code and solutions.ipynb with pre-filled code.
limitations: Simple prompting cannot answer questions outside pre-trained knowledge, handle complex queries, or provide personalized responses.
RAG does not equip LLMs to handle complex multi-step tasks or self-refine responses.
Agents come with higher cost and latency compared to simple prompting and RAG.
LLMs do not actually execute functions themselves; the execution must be implemented in the code.
Traditional multimodal data pipelines suffer from loss of context at chunk boundaries and pipeline complexity.
CLIP-based multimodal embedding models have a modality gap where irrelevant items of the same modality appear closer in vector space than relevant items of different modalities.
The screenshot-based approach is slightly better than chunking but still not ideal.
LLMs suffer from the 'lost in the middle' problem, so large context windows do not eliminate the need for targeted retrieval.
Weakly aligned modalities like time series data cannot easily share a vector space with text and images, requiring different retrieval strategies.
Not all LLMs or VLMs can run locally; model selection depends on hardware specifications.
quantitativeClaims: Three main paradigms for interacting with LLMs: simple prompting, RAG, and agents.
Two classes of multimodal machine learning models: multimodal embedding models and multimodal LLMs.
Two objectives for the agent: answering questions about a large document corpus and explaining or analyzing charts or diagrams.
Two modalities used in the lab: text and images.
The agent has one tool: a vector search tool for retrieving multimodal documents.
The lab provides approximately 45 minutes for coding, with about 10 minutes for setup.
Two notebook options are provided: lab.ipynb and solutions.ipynb.
